title: A Radio Call-In About Comparing Screen Time Numbers
script: Radio Host: [cheerfully] Good evening, listeners. Tonight we're discussing screen time reports, those weekly summaries our phones send us. We have a caller. Hello!
Caller: [a little nervous] Hello! I've actually wanted to talk about this for weeks, so thank you for taking my call tonight.
Radio Host: [curious] Tell us what happened. What made this topic worth calling about specifically?
Caller: [honestly] My weekly report said nine hours a day, and even though I suspected it was high, seeing the number felt like a small shock.
Radio Host: [interested] What was your first reaction when you actually saw that number written down?
Caller: [reflective] Honestly, defensiveness. I told myself half of that was work-related, checking emails and messages, so it didn't fully count.
Radio Host: [curious] Did you eventually accept that explanation, or did something make you question it further?
Caller: [thoughtful] I questioned it, once I checked the breakdown. Only two hours were work apps; the rest was scrolling, games, and videos I barely remembered watching.
Radio Host: [interested] That's a striking difference. How did that discovery change what you did afterward?
Caller: [explaining] Instead of deleting apps immediately, which never worked for me before, I set specific time limits for the ones eating up the most hours.
Radio Host: [curious] Did the limits actually work, despite how easy those limits usually are to simply ignore?
Caller: [honestly] The first week, I overrode them constantly. However, by week three, hitting the limit finally felt like a real, useful signal to stop.
Radio Host: [interested] What does your report look like now, compared to those original nine hours?
Caller: [warmly] About five hours, and much of that is genuinely intentional now, video calls with my parents, or music while cooking dinner.
Radio Host: [curious] What would you tell listeners who feel afraid to actually check their own number?
Caller: [encouraging] Check it anyway, even though it's uncomfortable. As a result, you can't fix a habit that you're still pretending doesn't exist.
Radio Host: [warmly] Wise advice. Thank you for being so honest with us and our listeners tonight.
Caller: [sincerely] Thank you for listening. I hope someone finally checks their own number after hearing this.
